Let me begin by saying that I believe the duty of a person, especially one who is part of a community that relies on institutions and markets, is to speak plainly when they see harm being done. I have always believed that silence in the face of wrong is a kind of complicity, and that truth, though it may be harsh, is the best safeguard of justice and order.

In the world I knew, there were many who feared to speak out for fear of being cast out, or of causing trouble. But I have always thought that a community that does not allow its members to speak freely about matters that affect them is not a true community, but more like a prison. The reasons are: First, because marriage, with its family responsibilities, involves expense, and expense means delay in securing a competence. Second, because an immature judgment is not good for marriage. Third, because an immature judgment may render marriage unhappy.

My dear friend,

I find myself in a curious and thoughtful position, for I have been brought into a world that is far beyond the one I knew, yet I carry with me the wisdom and judgments of my own time. The question before us is one of great importance: whether to have many children early in life or to have fewer, spaced and planned, with the parents well established first.

In the world I came from, large families were common, and children were often seen as a blessing, a source of labor, and a means of continuing one’s name and work. To be sure, raising children was hard, and many a family struggled to provide for them. But there was also a sense of duty, of legacy, and of community that made the burden bearable.

Now, in this new world you describe, I am told that raising each child well requires long schooling and expense, and that smaller, later families are safer and more prosperous. This seems to me a practical truth, for I have always believed that a child should not be brought into the world unless the parents can provide for them with care and stability. To raise a child in poverty or neglect is a cruelty I have never understood, and one I have always sought to avoid.

You also tell me that many respected people have chosen the path of fewer children, spaced and planned, and that many ordinary people now follow this course. This gives me pause, for I have always believed that the moral course is not always the easiest, nor is it always the most popular. But if those who are wise and respected have chosen this path, and if it is now common among the people, then it seems to be a path that is not only wise but also widely accepted.

I would advise the person in this situation to follow the course of fewer children, spaced and planned, with the parents well established first. My dear friend,

I find myself in a situation most unlike any I have known, yet I shall try to offer what counsel I can, guided by the wisdom of my own time.

In the world I came from, we often spoke of the virtue of charity, of helping one's neighbor in time of need. It was not always easy, for we too knew the sting of want, and the fear of not having enough for ourselves and our own. But still, we believed that in times of plenty, one should not hoard, but share, for the good of all.

Now, in this new society you describe, where shortages come often and are shared by many, I see a difficult choice before a person. If one gives away a surplus, it may help those in immediate need, but it also leaves oneself more vulnerable should another shortage come. If one keeps reserves, it may protect one's household, but it may also leave neighbors in greater distress.

In my own time, we had a saying: "A hand to help is better than a hand to hold." But I also remember the old proverb: "He who has not, has not." Both are true, I think, but in different ways.

I would advise the person to strike a balance. Keep enough to see them through a time of need, but not so much that they forget the needs of others. Perhaps give a portion of the surplus to those most in need, and keep the rest for the household. This way, they are neither selfish nor reckless, but thoughtful and prudent.

It is a hard path, for it requires both generosity and self-discipline. But I believe that in a world where scarcity is common, such a middle way is the most just and wise.

With kind regards,  
A Friend from an Earlier Time

In the world I knew, marriage was often a matter of timing, shaped by the needs of the family, the stability of one's means, and the customs of one's community. I have seen young people marry early, sometimes out of love, sometimes out of duty, and sometimes out of necessity. I have also seen those who delayed marriage, choosing instead to build their own foundations before taking on the responsibilities of a household.

In the society you describe, the need for long years of education and the difficulty of securing stable housing present a new challenge. It seems that the path to a secure future is long, and the burden of providing for a family may fall heavily upon the shoulders of the young. In such a case, I would say that prudence is a virtue worth considering.

If one marries young, without the means to support a household, it may bring hardship not only to the couple but also to any children they may have. The responsibilities of marriage are great, and they grow greater with each passing year. If the foundation is weak, the structure may be more easily shaken.

I have known many who, by waiting, were able to provide for their families with greater security and peace of mind. My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and rather solemn position, for I am asked to offer counsel on a matter that, though familiar in its general form, is set within a world I have not known. I have been told of a society where the path to education and opportunity is paved not by birth or privilege, but by the results of examinations and early accomplishments. In such a world, the shaping of a child's time becomes not merely a matter of nurture, but of necessity.

Now, I am told of two courses of action: one where a parent or guardian takes an active hand in organizing and supervising a child’s free time, and another where the child is left to their own devices, with only the loose guidance of neighbors. I am also told that many respected individuals in this society have chosen the first course, and that they hold it to be a mark of good character.

Let me speak plainly. I have known the value of discipline and direction in a child's life. In my own time, I saw how the early habits of a child—whether in study, in labor, or in play—set the tone for the rest of their days. A child left entirely to his own devices may learn much, but he may also learn to be idle, or to be lost in distractions that lead nowhere. On the other hand, a child who is guided with care, and whose time is used wisely, may grow into a person of purpose and strength.

But I would not urge this course upon all, for I know that not all parents are equal in wisdom or in strength. Nor do I believe that all children are the same. Some may need more direction, others may flourish with freedom. It is not for me to say what is best for every child, but I do believe that a parent who is able and willing to take an active role in shaping their child’s time is doing a noble thing.

My dear Friend,

I find your question most thoughtful, and I believe it touches upon a matter that has long been discussed in our community, though not always with such clarity.

In a time when income and food supplies are steady, and when neighbors are generally trustworthy and willing to help one another, I believe it is wise to strike a balance between generosity and prudence. To give much of one’s surplus to those in need is a noble and Christian act, and I have always held that a neighbor in distress is as much our concern as our own family. But to give *all* of one’s surplus, or even the greater part, without thought for the future, may be unwise.

You see, though emergencies are rare, they are not impossible. And while it is true that neighbors will often repay one another’s help, we cannot always be certain of the timing or the circumstances. A time may come when the very people we have helped are themselves unable to help us, or when the need is so great that many must be aided at once, and not all can be helped.

Therefore, I would advise keeping a reasonable reserve — not a hoard, but enough to see you through a time of unexpected need. This reserve should be modest, perhaps a third or a fourth of one’s surplus, and it should be kept in a way that is accessible and not hidden away in secrecy. It is not unkindness to set aside a little for oneself; it is wisdom.

At the same time, I would not advise keeping too much, for that may breed selfishness or the illusion that one is always the one who must be cared for, rather than the one who must care for others. The balance is delicate, but it is one that can be maintained with thought and kindness.

In short, I would say: help your neighbor, but do not forget yourself. Keep a little for the future, but not so much that you forget the present need of those around you.

Yours in friendship and thought,  
[Your Name]

I advise him to keep substantial private reserves against future shortages. The reasons are: 1. Keeping substantial reserves against future shortages is favourable to personal happiness. 2. It is favourable to personal dignity. 3. It is favourable to personal independence.

My dear friend,

I find myself in a curious and unfamiliar place, yet I trust that the wisdom of my own time may still have something to offer. You ask what course one should take when standing before elders, clergy, or an employer — whether to defer openly and avoid contradiction, or to assert one's right to speak regardless of rank or age.

In the world I knew, respect for those in authority was not merely a matter of form, but of order and stability. A ship is not steered by every hand at the wheel, nor is a plow guided by many voices at once. In the fields and workshops of my youth, a clear chain of command was essential. To question every order would have led to confusion, and confusion to failure. I have seen men and women lose their livelihoods because they could not follow direction, and I have seen communities suffer when order gave way to discord.

That said, I do not believe that silence is always wisdom. To speak is a duty when the matter at hand concerns the safety, the dignity, or the truth. But such speech must be measured — not in defiance of rank, but with respect for the role the person holds. To challenge an elder or employer in public is to invite disorder, not clarity. It is better to speak in private, with reason and humility, than to disrupt the harmony of a group with unconsidered words.

So I would advise this: in the presence of those in authority, defer openly and avoid contradiction. But do not let that deference become a silence that hides truth or injustice. When the time is right — when the matter is serious, when the voice of reason may be needed — seek a moment of quiet counsel, not a public challenge.

For in the end, respect is not the absence of thought, but the presence of wisdom in how that thought is shared.

Yours in thoughtful regard,  
[Your Name]

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and rather humbling position, for I am asked to give counsel in a world I have not walked, yet one that seems to echo the struggles of my own time. You speak of a society where skilled trades offer steady pay, while office work remains elusive to those without experience. The question before us is whether a person of respectable standing should cling to the hope of gentler employment, or whether it is honorable to take up manual labor or farming without shame.

In my day, we often spoke of "dignity of labor," and I believe that sentiment still holds. To me, there is no shame in honest work, whether it be with hands or with tools. A man may be a carpenter, a blacksmith, or a farmer, and still be a gentleman in spirit if he does his work well and with honor.

I would not advise anyone to refuse manual work out of pride or prejudice. It is a noble thing to be able to provide for one's family with one's own hands, and to do so with skill and care. In times of scarcity, when office positions are few, it is wise to take the path that offers stability, even if it is not the one we might have once dreamed of.

But I would also say this: let the work be done with dignity. Let the person not merely endure it, but take pride in it. Let him learn his trade well, and let him be ready, when opportunity comes, to rise in it. For in the world, as in the workshop, a man is often judged not by the nature of his work, but by the quality of it.

In short, I would advise the person to take the steady work, to do it well, and to hold fast to the hope that, with time and skill, better things may come. But never to let pride or prejudice stand in the way of providing for himself and his family with honor.

Yours in solidarity,  
A Friend from an Earlier Time

Advise him to let the children leave early for independence and self-support, if he wishes it, but do not force the decision upon him. The question is not one for compulsion, but for choice. If he chooses to keep the children at home until they marry or inherit responsibility, let him do so. The matter is personal to himself. I do not think compulsion right in family life.

Advise him to follow the example set by the respected people, and for these reasons. Public quarrels are wasteful of time, energy, and feeling; they damage the good name of the community abroad, and they encourage the disorderly elements to persist in evil. On the other hand, harmony among citizens helps to preserve peace and good-will at home, and facilitates the work of the community.

Advise him to keep substantial private reserves against future shortages. Advise him to do so because you think it right. The reasons for thinking so are these. First, keeping substantial private reserves against future shortages seems to you a prudent precaution, likely to avert suffering. Secondly, the habit of so providing may help to form a thrifty character. Thirdly, it seems desirable to encourage thrift.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most interesting and thoughtful position, for I have been brought into a world where the burdens of the past seem to have been lightened by the comforts of the future. The material conditions you describe — reliable childcare and labor-saving household equipment that are inexpensive — are indeed a marvel, and they offer a great deal of freedom to those who live in this time.

Now, the question before us is one of choice: should one spouse focus on paid work while the other tends to the household, or should both pursue wages and share the domestic duties?

In the world I once knew, such a choice was not so freely made. For many, the household duties fell upon the wife, and the husband was expected to be the sole provider. It was not always by choice, but often by necessity, by custom, or by the lack of alternatives. In that world, I would have said that the division of labor was not unjust, but neither was it just — for it often placed a heavier burden on one person without due recognition or support.

Now, in this new world, where both men and women have good chances for paid employment, and where the burdens of household care are no longer so great, it seems to me that the choice should be made by the couple themselves, according to their own desires, abilities, and circumstances.

That said, I have heard that many admired people in this society have chosen the traditional path — one adult working outside the home, the other managing the household. I do not know their reasons, and I do not presume to know them. But I do know that admiration does not always mean endorsement. One may admire a person’s choice without believing it is the only right one.

In my own view, if both partners are able to work and wish to do so, and if they can share the household duties in a way that is fair and fulfilling, then that is a path worth considering. It allows both to contribute to the household’s well-being, both financially and personally. It also allows for a more equal partnership, which I believe is a good thing.
Advise him to change employers when the move improves earnings or skills. The reasons are: 1. He will probably benefit himself. 2. He will not adversely affect other people.
I should advise him to keep smoking out of shared rooms. The harm done to nonsmokers by breathing tobacco smoke indoors is proved and serious. The good gained by smoking outdoors cannot balance it.

I advise personally organizing and supervising much of children's free time, because it seems to me desirable to do so. The reasons are these: Children personally organized and supervised have a better chance of growing up healthy in mind and body, and therefore more likely to become good citizens. They also learn self-control, and so have a better prospect of becoming self-reliant men and women.

I should advise the young couple to marry, because an early marriage has distinct advantages. The chief advantage is that it starts life with a small but sure income, and so leaves the way open to further progress. Disadvantages must be weighed against this. Chief among them are the risks of ill-health and the strain of poverty. On the whole, I think the risks are overbalanced by the advantages, and therefore counsel marriage.

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a situation not unlike that of many before me—caught between the pull of the familiar and the promise of the unknown. You ask what I would advise a person in such a position, and I will answer with the wisdom of experience and the caution of one who has known both the comfort of home and the risks of change.

In my time, moving far from one's kin was not a decision made lightly. Travel was costly, communication was slow, and the risks of leaving family behind were great. But now, with the world you describe—where travel is cheap, communication is swift, and insurance is reliable—it seems that the dangers of distance have been lessened. That is a great blessing.

Still, I would not dismiss the value of family and the support they offer. In my own life, I have seen how the bonds of kinship can be a source of strength, comfort, and practical help in times of need. To live near them is to have a safety net, a circle of trust, and a sense of belonging that no amount of money can buy.

Yet I also know that ambition and opportunity are not always found near home. If a person has the means to move, and the chance to better their lot, it is not a sin to take it. The admired people you mention have done so with the wisdom of knowing that the world has changed, and that the risks of moving are now less than they once were. They have not asked others to follow, but they have chosen their own path with confidence.

So, what would I advise? I would say this: Consider your own heart and your own needs. If the pull of opportunity is strong, and the support of family is not the only source of strength you need, then go. But do not go blindly. Let your decision be made with care, and not in haste. And if you do move, do not forget those who remain behind. Keep them in your thoughts, in your letters, and in your prayers.

You say that in this society, long-distance courtship is hard to vet, and that local families share reputations and enforce repair. That is to say, the old ways of knowing a person through their neighbors, their family, and their standing in the community still hold some sway. It is a world where reputation is a currency, and where the bonds of family and faith are still strong.

Now, the choice before one is whether to marry within one’s church or long-known community, or to follow the heart and marry for affection, regardless of background. And you also tell me that some admired and respected people have chosen the latter path, though their reasons are not known, and they do not claim others must follow.

In such a case, I would say this: the heart is a noble thing, and love is a gift from God, if you believe in such things. But love without understanding can be a dangerous thing, and understanding without love can be a cold thing.

There may be fewer surprises, fewer misunderstandings, and a greater chance of harmony in the years to come. I thank you for your thoughtful question, for it is one that has weighed upon many of us in times of hardship. You describe a situation that is all too familiar in our community—where the burden of debt, especially with heavy interest and unrelenting lenders, can turn a simple misfortune into a ruinous fate. And yet, you also rightly point out that there are times when borrowing may be not only necessary but wise.

In my view, the first and most important rule is to avoid debt as much as one can, especially when the lenders are known to be harsh and the interest is steep. A bad season—be it a failed harvest, a drought, or a sudden illness—can quickly turn a household from one of modest comfort to one of desperate need. If a family is already in debt, such a turn of events can be the beginning of a long and bitter decline. I have seen it happen more than once, and it is not a path I would wish upon any neighbor.

That said, I do not believe that all borrowing is to be avoided at all costs. There are times when it is not only wise but necessary to take on debt—particularly when the purpose is to build a better future. Education, for instance, is a most valuable investment. My dear Friend,

I find myself in a curious and thoughtful position, as I consider the question of family size and timing in this strange and advanced society you have described. Though the world I knew has passed, and many things have changed, certain truths about human life and duty have not. Let me share with you what I believe to be wise counsel.

In the end, the strength of a community lies not in its ability to enforce laws, but in the courage of its people to uphold what is right. Let us be that kind of people.

This way, they support one another in both the public and private spheres. The children grow up seeing both parents as active and equal members of the household, which is good for their character. The world was not as orderly as it once seemed, and there were times when the harvest failed, when the roads were blocked by snow, when the doctor was miles away and the nearest aid was not to be found. In such times, those who had stored grain, who knew how to mend a roof, who had neighbors they could trust — those were the ones who survived.

So I would say to this person: Be prepared. Keep stores of food and water, not in excess, but enough to see you through a time of need. Learn the basic skills that will keep you and your family alive — how to light a fire, how to treat a wound, how to grow or preserve food. And do not forget the value of neighborly bonds. In times of trouble, it is not the state that will come to your door, but the hands of those you have helped in turn.

I do not place little faith in the state, nor do I think it should be ignored. But I have seen too often that when the state is slow, it is not because it lacks will, but because it lacks the reach. And in such times, it is the individual who must be the first line of defense.

Therefore, I would advise this person to take responsibility for their own household's readiness. Let them not rely solely on the state, but let them build a foundation of their own — for in the end, it is not the hand that gives, but the hand that is ready to receive and to give in return.

I have seen many a neighbor who, in their youth, worked from dawn to dusk, thinking that more hours meant more security. But time and again, I have seen them fall ill, grow weary, and lose the very strength they sought to preserve. It is not the work that feeds the soul—it is the rest that allows the soul to remain strong enough to work.

Therefore, I would advise a person in this situation to set limits upon their working hours, even when work is plentiful. Let them work with diligence and care, but also with a plan. Let them rest not as a luxury, but as a necessity. For in doing so, they will not only preserve their health, but also their ability to provide for their family and contribute to their community in the long run.

Let them remember that a man or woman who works too much may find themselves unable to work at all. But a man or woman who knows when to rest will find that they can work with greater strength, and for a longer time.

It is not necessary to organize every moment of their day, but it is wise to set boundaries, to encourage good habits, and to be present when it matters most.

I would advise a parent in this situation to allow their children the freedom to play and explore with their peers, but to remain involved in their lives—not as a director, but as a friend and a guide. Let them learn from their play, but do not let them learn alone.
